\section[il pane]{il pane — bread, and its companions}

\label{lesson:IT-C11-pane}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} \textbf{il pane} (\textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{}) — and, true to form, Italian keeps it \textbf{closest to Latin}: \emph{pānis $\to$ pane}, barely touched. Its root carries the same warm story as the French \emph{pain}: a \textbf{companion} is one you \textbf{share bread} with.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{il pane} (\textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{pānis} — masculine, \emph{il} pane; the plural is \emph{i pani}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{companion / company} $\leftarrow$ \emph{com-} (\textquotedblleft{}with\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{pānis} — \textquotedblleft{}one you \textbf{break bread with}.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{pantry}, \textbf{pannier} (a bread-basket).
  \item And a purely Italian gem: \textbf{companatico} — the word for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{whatever you eat with bread}\textquotedblright{} (cheese, salami, anything on it). The bread is the given; the \emph{companatico} is what joins it — the same \emph{com- + pānis} idea, alive in one Italian word.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\section[l'acqua, il vino]{l'acqua, il vino — water and wine, close to the source}

\label{lesson:IT-C11-acqua-vino}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} The Italian table's two drinks — and a neat contrast with French. Where French dissolved Latin \emph{aqua} into a bare \textbf{eau} (\textquotedblleft{}oh\textquotedblright{}), Italian kept it almost \textbf{whole}: \textbf{acqua}, with the \emph{aqua} still ringing in it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{l'acqua} (\textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{aqua}. Italian barely moved it — it even \textbf{doubles} the sound with \textbf{-cq-} (\emph{AH-kwa}), holding onto the hard \emph{qu} that French threw away. Set them side by side: Latin \emph{aqua} $\to$ Italian \textbf{acqua} (kept) vs French \textbf{eau} (worn to a vowel). English borrowed the same loud original for \textbf{aquatic, aquarium, aqueduct}. Takes \emph{l'} before the vowel.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{il vino} (\textquotedblleft{}wine\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{vīnum} — clean and close, like everything Italian. The same word travelled into English as \textbf{wine}, and gives \textbf{vine, vinegar, vintage, vineyard, vinyl}. Masculine: \emph{il} vino.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}l'acqua, il vino\textquotedblright{} — \emph{acqua} with the doubled \emph{-cq-}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}Latin \emph{aqua} $\to$ Italian \textbf{acqua} (kept), French \textbf{eau} (worn away)\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}acqua $\leftrightarrow$ aquarium; vino $\to$ wine, vinegar\textquotedblright{}{]}
\end{itemize}
